posts.title: Fourteen new arrivals, and the three we'd take on a long train
posts.excerpt: Wednesday's boxes brought fourteen new books to the front table. Here are the three we keep pressing on people, and why.
posts.content:
The boxes come on Wednesday mornings, before the shutter goes up. This week there were fourteen new books, which is about as many as the front table can hold without someone having to move the cat.

We read a good half of each before it goes out. Most get a hand-written shelf card. Three of them got an argument, which is how you know.

The three for a long train

  • A Field Guide to Empty Stations, Sayo Minegishi. Twenty-two walks through stations where nobody gets off. Read one per stop.
  • Eleven Bridges in the Rain, Tomoe Hasunuma. A postman, a river city and one very long wet season. You'll miss your stop.
  • The Indigo Year, Aki Tanemura. Fifty-two short poems; it fits in a coat pocket and lasts all the way to the coast.

And the rest of the box

Two new translations from the Baltic, a cookbook written entirely in letters, a reissued collection of mountain essays, a very small book about very small birds, and the seventh issue of Spine Talk, the zine about bookbinding that we can never keep in stock.

A good front table should look slightly too full. Then you know somebody chose it.

Mariko Aoyagi

Everything is on the shelf this week. Ask at the counter, or write and we'll keep a copy for you.

posts.title: Setting the cover for The Indigo Year
posts.excerpt: Two colours, one platen and four days of the back room smelling of ink: how the cover of our ninth pocket book was made.
posts.content:
The Indigo Year is the ninth book from Shiori Press, and the first one whose cover we set entirely in wood type. The letters came out of a drawer we had not opened since we bought the press.

Two colours, at most

Our covers are printed in two colours or fewer, because that is all the platen can do in a day without the colours arguing. For The Indigo Year it was an indigo mixed to match a dyer's sample, and the kinari of the paper itself.

  • Paper: a 210 gsm kinari board, uncoated, from a mill in the north
  • Ink: one indigo, mixed by hand, eleven tries
  • Run: 800 covers, of which 31 went in the recycling

The book goes on sale at the counter on the first of October. The first hundred copies come with a bookmark printed from the offcuts.

posts.title: What happened at the zine clinic
posts.excerpt: Twelve people, one long-arm stapler and a guillotine: what got made at September's zine clinic, and what we learned about folding.
posts.content:
Twelve people came to September's zine clinic, which is two more than the long table can really hold. Nobody minded. By nine o'clock there were nineteen finished zines, a bent stapler and a new rule about the guillotine.

Three things we learned

  • Fold first, then write. Pages you plan flat never line up once folded.
  • Eight pages is a zine. Twelve is an ambition. Sixteen is a book, and you should come to the bookbinding evening.
  • Everyone's first zine is about their cat. That's fine.

The next clinic is on Thursday 23 October. Bring ten pages, or nothing at all, and leave with something stapled.

posts.title: A reading list for the first cold night
posts.excerpt: Five books for the evening you first need the heater: short, warm, and best read with the window just slightly open.
posts.content:
Every year there is one evening when the shop suddenly needs the heater, and people start asking for something to read in bed. This is the list we hand them.

  • The Indigo Year, Aki Tanemura. One poem for each week a dye vat is kept alive. Read one, turn the light off.
  • Night Laundry on Kasuga Street, Kei Moriwaki. Stories from an all-night launderette, warm as a dryer.
  • Weather Report from a Small Island, Noa Shirane, translated by Ilse Varga. Poems you can read aloud to someone already asleep.
  • A Field Guide to Empty Stations, Sayo Minegishi. For when you can't sleep and want to walk somewhere in your head.
  • Spine Talk No. 7. Because a zine about bookbinding is the best excuse to stay up.

Short books for long nights. That's the whole rule.

The counter

All five are on the front table until the end of October.

posts.title: Translating weather: notes from Ilse Varga
posts.excerpt: Our press editor on carrying an island's weather words into English, and why some poems needed three tries and a fishing almanac.
posts.content:
Noa Shirane's poems are about the weather on one small island, and the island has more words for wind than English has for anything. Ilse Varga spent a year translating forty of them for Shiori Press.

The hardest word was the one for the wind that comes just before the ferry is cancelled. In the end I used the ferry.

Ilse Varga

Three tries and an almanac

Some poems went through three complete versions. For the sea poems Ilse borrowed a fishing almanac from the island's one bookshop, and read it cover to cover to learn how the people there talk about the sky.

Ilse reads from the book at Translation Night on Thursday 30 October. There is a waiting list; write to the counter and we'll put your name on it.

posts.title: Why every book leaves wrapped in kinari
posts.excerpt: The unbleached paper, the cotton tie and the little slip inside: a short history of how a book leaves Shiori-do.
posts.content:
Since 1974 every book sold here has left wrapped in kinari, the unbleached off-white paper that the first owner bought by the roll from a stationer across the river. We still buy it from the same family.

Inside each parcel there is a slip: the date, the shelf the book came from, and a line from whoever wrapped it. That slip is where our newsletter got its name.

  • Paper: unbleached, 70 gsm, from a stationer across the river
  • Tie: cotton, natural or indigo
  • Slip: printed on the platen, written on by hand

We now sell the paper too, as a letter set, for people who asked once too often.

posts.title: Eleven bridges, one postman: notes from the August reading
posts.excerpt: Tomoe Hasunuma read the third chapter of her novel to a full counter, and then the rain started. Notes from a wet Thursday.
posts.content:
Tomoe Hasunuma read the third chapter of Eleven Bridges in the Rain to twelve chairs, a bench and four people standing by the poetry shelf. Halfway through, it started raining, which felt arranged.

Afterwards she talked about postmen, about the eleven real bridges she walked across while writing, and about why the book has no chapter set on a sunny day.

I wanted a city where you always have to cross water to get home.

Tomoe Hasunuma

Signed copies are on the front table. She reads again on Thursday 16 October; reserve a chair on the events page.

products.name: A Field Guide to Empty Stations
products.short: Twenty-two short walks through railway stations where nobody gets off, by Sayo Minegishi. Shiori Bunko No. 014.
products.description:
Sayo Minegishi spent two years getting off trains at the stations everyone else stays on for. This is the field guide she kept: twenty-two walks, each a few pages long, through waiting rooms, overgrown platforms and the one ticket office still run by the same man since the line opened.

Pocket bunko size, letterpress cover, sewn binding. Read one per stop.

products.name: Eleven Bridges in the Rain
products.short: A postman, a river city and one very long wet season. A novel by Tomoe Hasunuma; signed copies while they last.
products.description:
Every morning Toru crosses eleven bridges to deliver the post, and every morning it rains. When a letter arrives with no address but a drawing of the twelfth bridge, the one the city pulled down before he was born, his route begins to change.

The counter's favourite novel this autumn. Signed by the author at our August reading.

products.name: The Indigo Year
products.short: Fifty-two poems, one for every week a dye vat is kept alive, by Aki Tanemura. Shiori Bunko No. 009, letterpress cover.
products.description:
Aki Tanemura's grandmother kept an indigo vat alive for forty years. These fifty-two short poems follow one year of feeding it, stirring it, and waiting for the blue to come.

Cover set in wood type and printed on our platen in one hand-mixed indigo. The first hundred copies come with a letterpress bookmark.

products.name: Night Laundry on Kasuga Street
products.short: Nine stories set around one all-night launderette, by Kei Moriwaki. Funny, then not, then funny again.
products.description:
A night-shift nurse, a boy with one sock, two retired rivals and a launderette owner who never sleeps: nine linked stories that all happen between midnight and the first train.

Warm as a dryer. Our most-recommended book for anyone who says they don't read short stories.

products.name: Weather Report from a Small Island
products.short: Forty weather poems by Noa Shirane, translated by Ilse Varga. Shiori Bunko No. 027.
products.description:
The island has more words for wind than English has for anything. Noa Shirane's forty poems record a year of its weather, and Ilse Varga's translation carries them across with the help of a fishing almanac and a great deal of patience.

Bilingual notes at the back explain the weather words that would not travel.

products.name: Spine Talk No. 7
products.short: The seventh issue of the zine about bookbinding: stab stitches, coptic spines and a centrefold of endpapers. Risograph, two colours.
products.description:
Spine Talk is made by three binders who meet at our zine clinic. Issue seven covers Japanese stab binding, a coptic spine you can sew on the train, and a centrefold of twelve endpapers to cut out and use.

Printed on a risograph in blue and persimmon; no two covers are registered quite the same.

products.name: Shiori Press Almanac 2026
products.short: Twelve readings, twelve months: the press's yearbook, with a calendar of the counter's evenings and a story for each month.
products.description:
Our yearbook: a calendar of the year's readings with room to write, a short new story for each month from writers on our list, and a fold-out map of the second-hand row.

Launch price until the end of November.

products.name: Bunko Notebook, Indigo
products.short: A pocket notebook in the bunko size: 160 kinari pages, indigo cloth cover, a ribbon to keep your place.
products.description:
The same size as our pocket books, so it slips into the same pocket. 160 pages of smooth kinari paper with a faint dot grid, a sewn binding that lies flat, and an indigo cloth cover that softens with use.

Made for us by a binder two streets away.

products.name: Letterpress Bookmarks, Set of Six
products.short: Six narrow bookmarks printed on our platen press from cover offcuts, each with a cotton tassel.
products.description:
Printed from the offcuts of our covers, so each set is a small history of the press. Six bookmarks, two inks, cotton tassels in indigo and persimmon.

Every parcel from the shop already has one; these are for people who lend books out.

products.name: Kinari Letter Set
products.short: Twenty sheets of the unbleached kinari paper we wrap every book in, with ten envelopes and an indigo band.
products.description:
The same unbleached paper our books have been wrapped in since 1974, cut to letter size and lightly ruled. Twenty sheets, ten envelopes, held together with an indigo paper band.

For people who asked once too often where the wrapping paper comes from.
